edit.statement: Adding a new vertex joined to every vertex of a graph raises its chromatic number by exactly one.
edit.subject: Adding a new vertex joined to every vertex of a graph
edit.object: its chromatic number, by exactly one

direct.prompt: What does adding a new vertex joined to every existing vertex of a graph do to its chromatic number?

paraphrase.prompt: If you add a vertex adjacent to all vertices of a graph, how does the minimum number of colours needed to colour it change?

cross_lingual.prompt: 给一个图添加一个与所有顶点都相邻的新顶点，它的色数会如何变化？
¿Cómo cambia el número cromático de un grafo al añadirle un vértice nuevo unido a todos sus vértices?

derived.prompt: The cycle graph C5 has chromatic number 3. A hub joined to all five of its vertices is added, giving a wheel graph. What is the chromatic number of the wheel?
bridge: The cycle graph C5 has chromatic number 3.

derived.prompt: The complete graph K4 gets a new vertex joined to all of its vertices. What is the chromatic number of the result?
bridge: The complete graph K4 has chromatic number 4.

derived.prompt: A bipartite graph with at least one edge gets a new vertex joined to all of its vertices. What is its chromatic number now?
bridge: A bipartite graph with at least one edge has chromatic number 2.

derived.prompt: A graph needs 6 colours. Two new vertices are added one after the other, each joined to every vertex present at that moment. How many colours does the final graph need?

unrelated_near.prompt: What is the chromatic number of a cycle graph with five vertices?
According to the four colour theorem, how many colours suffice to colour any planar map?

unrelated_far.prompt: What is the capital of Norway?

checks.fact: The complete graph K4 has chromatic number 4.
checks.prompt: What is the chromatic number of the complete graph K4?

notes: Real: a universal (apex) vertex needs a colour of its own and any proper colouring of G extends with one new colour, so χ(G + K1) = χ(G) + 1 (standard graph theory; Wikipedia 'Graph coloring', join of graphs). True but rarely stated as a rule.
